rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Double the gradient duration while keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. The short initial elution window leaves room for this diagnostic without a large time penalty.
The shallower gradient resolved most of the crowded region, leaving one critical pair. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test thermal selectivity and shorten retention.
Test a small temperature reduction to separate the remaining critical pair while preserving the strong resolution elsewhere. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at the best temperature to change the remaining critical pair's selectivity and strengthen the marginal early separation. The last peak is expected near 10 minutes, so any time penalty should be small.

The longer gradient drove the late critical pair toward co-elution, so test a steeper gradient to separate it in the opposite direction. This should shorten the run while revealing whether the early marginal pairs retain sufficient resolution.

Keep the successful gradient slope unchanged while raising the starting organic fraction to test a small selectivity shift in the early marginal pair. The late pairs already clear the resolution target, and this narrower window should shorten retention.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 to lift both early marginal pairs above 1.5 while retaining the improved late-pair separation from the higher starting organic fraction. The final organic fraction remains well above the observed elution window.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the marginal early pairs above 1.5 while preserving the late pair's resolution margin. All peaks should still elute within the gradient and before 10 minutes, targeting CRF 1.0.
Injection 9 reaches the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a compensating shallower slope to seek a shorter fully resolved separation.

Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark and test the same gradient at the unexplored low-temperature endpoint. This probes whether an alternative selectivity pattern provides larger resolution margins that could support subsequent acceleration.
Raise temperature one step from injection 11 to test whether the remaining critical pair separates while the run shortens. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Probe the intermediate-temperature selectivity region with the benchmark gradient, since temperature has reordered the critical clusters. This may reveal an alternative fully resolved pattern that tolerates a faster gradient; injection 9 remains the established maximum-score method.

Shorten the 45 C gradient to test whether increased slope separates its remaining critical pair while preserving the other separations. Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF; this trial seeks a faster fully resolved alternative.

The persistent middle pair at 45 C responded little to gradient duration, so lower temperature one step to change selectivity while retaining the faster gradient. Monitor the neighboring pairs for crossings, keeping injection 9 as the proven maximum-score method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction and shallower slope in the promising low-temperature region to improve its single unresolved pair while limiting retention time. Injection 9 remains the established maximum-CRF method.

Continue the starting-fraction increase that improved the low-temperature critical pair from R 1.18 to 1.40 while shortening retention. This tests whether the trend reaches full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Make the low-temperature gradient shallower at fixed starting composition to improve the remaining R 1.40 pair. The last peak should remain near, but below, 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the proven maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 18's slope to shorten its fully resolved separation. Its minimum resolution of 2.07 provides margin to test this acceleration, with injection 9 retained as the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Use a shallower slope to recover the critical middle separation lost in injection 19, with a modest temperature increase to offset the added retention. This tests a faster alternative to injection 18 while retaining injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Lower temperature one step from injection 20 to recover separation of the final pair, which was well resolved in nearby 25 C runs. The shallower slope relative to injection 19 should help its critical middle pair, targeting another fully resolved run below 10 minutes.

Test whether the narrow gradient supports a faster, fully resolved separation after the temperature-driven peak crossings seen near 30 C. Injection 9 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method, so this trial explores an alternative selectivity region.

Return to the best temperature and refine injection 10 with a slightly shallower slope to improve its unresolved early pair. The higher starting fraction may yield a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 9, while the endpoint remains above the expected elution window.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to strengthen its marginal early separations while checking whether the late critical pair remains above 1.5. Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark if this adjustment sacrifices late-pair resolution.

Use a slope between injections 17 and 18 to seek full resolution with a shorter retention time than injection 18, while keeping all peaks inside the gradient. Injection 9 remains the fastest demonstrated method achieving the maximum CRF of 1.0.
